When a model delegates with `delegate_to_agent` or a `delegation_tool()`, it
waits for the answer before it does anything else. Background tasks remove
the wait. The lead's model starts a task on a
[retained agent](retained-agents.html), gets a task ID straight away, and
keeps working. Later it collects whichever result is ready, sends the same
agent a follow-up, or cancels a task it no longer needs.

Use background tasks when the lead has useful work of its own to do while
specialists run, when it should act on the first result without waiting for
the rest, or when it may decide partway through that a task isn't needed.
If the model should simply ask and wait, a `delegation_tool()` is simpler;
see [Which kind of delegation](#which-kind-of-delegation) below.

Background tasks last only as long as the run that started them. For work
that should outlive the R process, see [Background jobs](background-jobs.html).

## Set it up

Retain each specialist, then give the lead the task tools with
`background_tools()`:

```{r}
library(deputy)

lead <- Agent$new(
  chat = ellmer::chat("anthropic/claude-sonnet-5"),
  system_prompt = "You write batch reports with help from two specialists.",
  usage_limits = UsageLimits(max_requests = 30)
)

analyst <- Agent$new(
  chat = ellmer::chat("openai/gpt-6-luna"),
  tools = tools_data(),
  permissions = permissions_readonly(),
  system_prompt = "You analyse measurement files and explain your reasoning."
)
reviewer <- Agent$new(
  chat = ellmer::chat("openai/gpt-6-luna"),
  tools = tools_preset("minimal"),
  permissions = permissions_readonly(),
  system_prompt = "You review draft reports against the style guide."
)

handles <- c(
  analyst = lead$retain_agent(analyst, UsageLimits(max_requests = 20)),
  reviewer = lead$retain_agent(reviewer, UsageLimits(max_requests = 20))
)

lead$register_tools(background_tools(
  lead,
  agents = handles,
  usage_limits = UsageLimits(max_requests = 5),
  descriptions = c(
    analyst = "Analyses the measurement files",
    reviewer = "Reviews draft reports"
  )
))

result <- lead$run_sync(
  "Report on batch 12: summarise measurements.csv and have draft.md reviewed."
)
```

The names of `agents` are what the model calls the specialists, and
`descriptions` tells it what each is for. Handles can also come from
`adopt_chat()`. `usage_limits` is the budget for each task; the limits given
to `retain_agent()` cap each specialist's total across all its tasks.

The model can't change any of this. It chooses a specialist by name and
writes the task; the agents, their tools, their permissions and the budgets
are fixed by your code.

## What the model sees

`background_tools()` returns five tools:

| Tool | What it does | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `task_start(agent, task)` | Starts a task for a specialist | A task ID, at once |
| `task_status(task_ids)` | Reports each task's state and progress | At once |
| `task_wait(task_ids, until)` | Waits for tasks and returns the finished ones' outcomes | When one task (`until = "any"`, the default) or every task (`"all"`) has finished |
| `task_follow_up(task_id, task)` | Sends another task to the specialist that ran `task_id` | A new task ID, at once |
| `task_cancel(task_id, reason)` | Asks a task to stop | The task's state, at once |

A typical run has the model call `task_start` once or more, do some work of
its own, and then call `task_wait`.

`task_wait` is a single tool call that stays open until a task finishes. The
lead makes no model request while it waits, so waiting costs nothing. It
returns every finished task the model hasn't collected yet, so tasks that
finish close together arrive in one result, and it lists the tasks still
running. Each finished task comes with the same compact
[outcome](delegation.html#what-a-delegation-returns) as an ordinary
delegation. If nothing is pending it returns at once and says so. Leaving out
`task_ids` waits on every task not yet collected.

A specialist runs one task at a time. A `task_start` or `task_follow_up` for
a busy specialist is `queued` and starts, in order, when the specialist is
free. A follow-up continues the specialist's conversation, so it can build on
the earlier task without being told everything again.

A task is in one of these states:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `queued` | Waiting for a busy specialist |
| `running` | The specialist is working |
| `cancelling` | Asked to stop, and finishing its current step |
| `completed` | The specialist finished normally |
| `failed` | The task ended with an error |
| `cancelled` | Stopped by `task_cancel` or because the lead's run ended |
| `stopped` | A limit or a hook ended it |
| `rejected` | Refused when its turn came; the reason is reported |

`completed` means the specialist finished, not that it did the task well.

Task IDs work only in the run that created them, and only through these
tools. A later run of the lead can't use an earlier run's IDs.

## What your code sees

`lead$background_tasks()` returns a data frame with one row per task of the
lead's current run, or its latest run when none is going:

```{r}
tasks <- lead$background_tasks()
tasks[, c("agent", "state", "collected", "previous_task_id")]
```

`collected` says whether the model read the result with `task_wait`, and
`previous_task_id` is set on a follow-up. A task the model cancelled has the
`stop_reason` `"cancelled"`, with the reason the model gave, if any, in
`cancel_note`; a task cancelled because the lead stopped has the lead's stop
reason, such as `"parent_completed"`. The rows stay until the lead's next
run starts.

Each task is an ordinary delegation, so the methods described in
[Briefing and inspecting subagents](delegation.html) work with the
`delegation_id` column:

```{r}
lead$list_subagents()

# Needs a DelegationDisclosure() on the lead that allows current_user.
lead$inspect_subagents(current_user, tasks$delegation_id[[1]], transcript = TRUE)

reader <- lead$observe_subagents(current_user)
reader$poll()$events
```

Give the lead a `DelegationDisclosure()` (the `delegation_disclosure` argument
of `Agent$new()`) to decide who may read specialists' conversations.
`observe_subagents()` shows tool calls and text as they happen, which is how
an app can show progress while the lead is busy. A follow-up's transcript
holds the specialist's whole conversation, earlier tasks included. A task
cancelled or rejected before its turn came never ran, so it has a row in
`background_tasks()` and nothing elsewhere.

A specialist keeps its own permissions, and each tool call it makes must also
pass the lead's permissions as they are at that moment, and the lead's
`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse` and `PostToolUseFailure` hooks. Narrowing the
lead's permissions with `set_permission_mode()` therefore applies to tasks
already running. A lead in read-only or plan mode can still use the task
tools, and its specialists are then held to that mode.

## Budgets

The lead and its tasks now spend at the same time, so each task's
`usage_limits` are set aside from the lead's run when the task starts. When
the task finishes, what it didn't use is returned and what it did use is
added to the run's usage. While a task runs, the lead's own requests and tool
calls can't use what is set aside. The lead and its tasks together therefore
stay within the run's request and tool-call limits, and `result$usage`
includes every task.

Three things follow:

- A `task_start` that would leave the lead nothing under one of its run's
  limits is refused, and the model is told why. With a lead limited to 30
  requests and 10 set aside per task, the model can have two tasks pending
  and still make requests of its own, but not three.
- Give `usage_limits` a value for each limit the lead's run has. If the lead
  has a `max_tool_calls` and the tasks don't, a task could use all of it, so
  every start is refused.
- Token and cost limits are checked after each response, because the size of
  a response isn't known in advance. The lead and each running task can each
  overshoot them by one response.

A task also can't exceed what its specialist has left of the budget given to
`retain_agent()`. `max_active` (default 4) caps how many tasks can be queued
or running at once, and `max_tasks` (default 16) caps the tasks in one run.
Starts beyond either are refused until a task finishes.

## When the lead stops

Tasks belong to the run that started them. When the lead's model stops, for
any reason (it answered, a limit was reached, you called `lead$interrupt()`,
or an error ended the run), Deputy cancels the tasks still queued, asks the
running ones to stop, and waits for them before the run returns. Nothing
keeps running after `run_sync()` returns or the promise from `run_async()`
resolves, and the run's usage is complete.

A model that answers without collecting a task therefore loses that task's
result. The task still appears in `lead$background_tasks()` with
`collected = FALSE`, and whatever the specialist did before it stopped stays
in its conversation.

Because the run waits for running tasks to stop, a specialist in the middle
of a slow tool call delays the lead's result until that call returns.

## Cancelling

`task_cancel` asks a task to stop. A queued task is removed and never starts.
A running task finishes the tool call it is in, then stops, and the work it
did so far stays in the specialist's conversation. Cancelling a task that
already finished changes nothing and reports the state it finished in.

Deputy can't interrupt a tool that is running, so a tool with side effects
completes them even when its task is cancelled.

Your own code can stop a task with `lead$interrupt_subagent(delegation_id)`,
or everything with `lead$interrupt()`.

## Limits

- The lead can't be part of a delegation graph made with
  `retain_agent_graph()`, as its root or as a member, and a retained agent
  can't start background tasks of its own.
- A lead with a `TrustedResults()` policy can't register the tools.
- Subagents defined with `agent_definition()` and reached through
  `delegate_to_agent` always block. A `LeadAgent` can have both: definitions
  for blocking delegation, and retained agents with background tools.
- Tasks, handles and conversations live in memory. They don't survive an R
  restart and can't run on a timer or after the run ends. Use
  [background jobs](background-jobs.html) for that.
- Register the tools only on the agent you passed as `owner`. Calling
  `background_tools()` again for the same agent replaces its task list, and
  is an error while tasks are pending.

## Which kind of delegation

| | Blocking: `delegate_to_agent`, `delegation_tool()` | Background: `background_tools()` | Batch: `parallel_delegate()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Started by | The model | The model | Your code |
| While the work runs | The lead waits for the answer | The lead keeps working, and waits when it chooses | The lead makes no request |
| Who does the work | A new subagent from a definition, or a retained agent | Retained agents | New subagents from definitions |
| Tools for the subagent | Yes | Yes | No, and one request each |
| Follow-up in the same conversation | With `delegation_tool()` | With `task_follow_up` | No |
| The model can cancel | No | Yes | No |

Choose blocking delegation when the lead needs the answer before it can do
anything else: it is the simplest for the model to use well. Choose
background tasks when the lead can make progress in the meantime or may not
need every result. Choose `parallel_delegate()` when your code, not the
model, decides to ask several subagents the same kind of question and each
can answer in one reply without tools.

## A complete example

The `background-tasks` example runs the whole sequence (two starts, the
lead's own tool call, a wait, a follow-up, a cancellation) and prints what
each of the methods above returns. It uses a local test server, so it needs
no API key:

```{r}
source(system.file("examples", "background-tasks", "run.R", package = "deputy"))
```
